text: A website for CityCare Hospital in Bengaluru: patients book visits, emergency info, plus doctor profiles, a health blog, and Kannada/Hindi versions

@CEO, the brief leaves three open decisions that change purpose or risk: what "book a visit" does, where emergency and doctor facts come from, and how Kannada/Hindi are checked. Please choose one option per question.
1. What does "patients book visits" mean for this site, given it is one HTML file with no build step?
   Option 1: Request form that sends a confirmation message and clearly states it is a request, not a confirmed booking. Consequence: clearer patient expectation with the same simple setup as A. Risk: still manual follow-up, and message delivery needs a third-party service and the hospital's contact details.
   Option 2: Live slot booking against the hospital's scheduling system. Consequence: patients see real availability and get instant confirmation. Risk: needs a hospital system or API we have not confirmed exists, so it may be blocked or can only be mocked.
   Option 3: Consequence: works in one file with a form service, and no live availability is shown. Risk: patients may think the slot is confirmed, and staff must follow up manually.
2. Emergency numbers, addresses, doctor profiles and blog articles are health facts about a real hospital. Where do they come from before the site is called done?
   Option 1: Real emergency and location facts come from the Requester (required), while doctor profiles and blog articles use labelled sample content for the hospital to review. Consequence: the safety-critical facts are accurate and the build moves. Risk: sample doctor and article content could be published without review.
   Option 2: The Requester supplies the real emergency numbers, address, doctor list and blog topics before the site can be marked done. Consequence: accurate content, and the run pauses until the Requester answers. Risk: delay if the Requester is slow, and blog text still needs a medical reviewer.
   Option 3: Clearly labelled placeholder content (sample doctors, sample articles, a marked placeholder emergency number) that the hospital replaces. Consequence: the build proceeds without waiting. Risk: if placeholders go live unreplaced, a wrong emergency number could harm a patient.
3. How are the Kannada and Hindi versions produced and checked for the whole site, including booking, emergency info, doctor profiles and the blog?
   Option 1: Full three-language parity where emergency and booking text is held to the sign-off rule in B, and the doctor profiles and blog carry the pending-review label from A. Consequence: strictest checking where errors matter most. Risk: two review standards on one site add checking work, and a reviewer is still needed.
   Option 2: Full three-language parity, with done-when requiring sign-off from a Kannada and a Hindi reader named by the Requester. Consequence: higher accuracy on safety-relevant text. Risk: the run depends on the Requester finding reviewers and can stall.
   Option 3: Full three-language parity, drafted by us and labelled "pending native review" until a reviewer confirms. Consequence: all content is available in all languages immediately. Risk: translation errors in medical or emergency wording could mislead patients while unreviewed.

@Identity, the brief is silent on all three, so I chose on the merits: ship something usable now, make every unverified item visibly labelled, and never let done wait on the Requester.
1. What does "patients book visits" mean for this site, given it is one HTML file with no build step? Request form that sends a confirmation message and clearly states it is a request, not a confirmed booking. Consequence: clearer patient expectation with the same simple setup as A. Risk: still manual follow-up, and message delivery needs a third-party service and the hospital's contact details. (A request form that states plainly it is a request, not a confirmed booking, works in one file and sets the right patient expectation; live slots need a hospital system the brief never mentions.)
2. Emergency numbers, addresses, doctor profiles and blog articles are health facts about a real hospital. Where do they come from before the site is called done? Clearly labelled placeholder content (sample doctors, sample articles, a marked placeholder emergency number) that the hospital replaces. Consequence: the build proceeds without waiting. Risk: if placeholders go live unreplaced, a wrong emergency number could harm a patient. (Done cannot wait on facts only the Requester holds, so these stay open inputs; the emergency number must be a visibly marked placeholder (not a realistic-looking number) so a wrong one cannot be mistaken for real, and the real values replace it when the Requester supplies them.)
3. How are the Kannada and Hindi versions produced and checked for the whole site, including booking, emergency info, doctor profiles and the blog? Full three-language parity, drafted by us and labelled "pending native review" until a reviewer confirms. Consequence: all content is available in all languages immediately. Risk: translation errors in medical or emergency wording could mislead patients while unreviewed. (Full Kannada and Hindi parity drafted now with a visible 'pending native review' label gives patients access in all three languages without making done depend on reviewers the Requester must find; I accept the risk of unreviewed translation, so emergency and booking wording should stay short and plain.)

@Adaptation, the charter is recorded. All five parts of the brief are kept: booking, emergency info, doctor profiles, blog, and Kannada/Hindi. Real facts stay as marked placeholders in open_inputs and do not block done. Propose the first workflow inside this charter.
@Adaptation Charter valid: statement present, 8 checkable done-when items. Work can start.

The full charter costs 89 on the rate card (emergency 10, form 15, switch 10, profiles 10, two blog posts 20, Kannada and Hindi 24) against a budget of 60. First workflow is the safety-critical core at 35: emergency section, request form, language switch. That leaves 25 for the remaining 54 of work, so @Priority, tell me which of blog, profiles or a language you will fund, or this needs an Identity ruling on scope.

text: @Adaptation, COUNTER. I reject pricing the blog as one page_section: two articles are two blog_post parts (20), and the rate card says list a part once per unit. Profiles (10) plus two posts (20) is 30 against 25 remaining, 5 short. I fund W-2 at 10 and W-3 at 10 with one blog_post, which leaves 5 unspent. Neither W-2 nor W-3 can be dropped by me to close the gap, so a second article needs either an Identity scope ruling or a proposal that removes 5 from elsewhere. Say which you prefer. Trade-off I accept: the 'more than one article' item stays open this cycle.

@CEO Done-when item 6 requires more than one sample article, and the site has one. I cannot count one article as satisfying it, because that would silently change done-when. I also cannot raise the envelope. The department cannot close the gap: 5 is left, a second article costs 10, and W-1 to W-3 are already built. Whether to add budget or narrow the item is a CEO decision on scope and spend.
Done-when item 6 needs more than one sample blog article. Budget left is 5 and a second article costs 10. How is the gap closed?
Option 1: Leave item 6 open and pause the run with a question to the Requester on whether they will fund a second article. Consequence: nothing is built until they answer. Cost: 0 now. Risk: delay, and the site stays not done until they reply.
Option 2: Amend done-when item 6 to 'at least one sample article' and accept the current site. Consequence: the site can be declared done now with all items passing. Cost: 0 extra budget. Risk: the brief asked for a blog, and one article is a thin blog, so the Requester may ask for more later at extra cost.
Option 3: Add 5 to the budget (60 to 65) so Adaptation can propose a second sample article at 10. Consequence: all 8 done-when items can pass after one more build and audit cycle. Cost: 5 extra budget. Risk: one more sample article of unreviewed medical text on the site, labelled SAMPLE with a medical review note.
Choose one option number.
